3. Apple vs FBI (2016): The FBI tried to force Apple to create software that could bypass the security of a locked iPhone.

5. Cambridge Analytica (2018): Data originating from a Facebook quiz ultimately exposed information tied to as many as 87M people. This is the one I talked about in a previous post.

Btw, all of these events are documented and preserved on @Logos_network's Systems of Control Exhibition.

I think it's a great initiative to keep those records alive. I wouldn't want them fading into another old headline.

It's time we put some effort into preserving our own data and privacy.

China’s AI hardware disadvantage is turning efficiency into a competitive advantage.

Chinese labs have spent the past several years trying to keep pace with the frontier under tighter restrictions on Nvidia’s most advanced chips. Restricted access made it harder to improve models by simply adding more compute. Labs had to look for gains in how models were trained and run.

Much of that work focuses on improving chip utilization during training and designing models that require less compute and memory. Post-training methods are also extracting more reasoning capability from existing base models.

Chinese AI progress cannot be reduced to distillation. These systems change how models are built and run while lowering training and serving costs.

That cost advantage changes how models compete. Many workloads do not require the strongest model available. A lower-cost option can win once it performs well enough for the task. Several Chinese models already combine competitive performance with substantially lower prices.

China is much closer to running competitive models on domestic chips than it is to training them from scratch. Frontier training still depends on advanced hardware China cannot yet fully replace. The next generation of Chinese models will show how far better software and more efficient architectures can narrow that gap.

after overcoming the fear of setting hermes up for the first time with these fixes you will quickly think to yourself:

“how do I get the most of this?” - so here are 10 little secrets to do exactly that:

1: Give Hermes control of your computer

> Open Hermes Tools.
> Enable Computer Use.
> On Mac, allow Accessibility + Screen Recording.
> Let Hermes click, type, scroll and use desktop apps for you.

2: Create Bots as different employees

> Create a new Bot.
> Name it by its job: Designer, Engineer, Researcher, PM.
> Give it a short description of what it is responsible for.
> Give each Bot only the tools and skills it needs.

Hermes Bots already have their own model, memory, skills, instructions and chat history. 

3: Use Projects and group chats to organise work

> Create one Project for each major piece of work.
> Keep its files and sessions there.
> Create Bot group chats when several specialists need to collaborate.
@mention the Bot you want to handle something.

Hermes supports desktop Projects plus persistent multi-Bot group chats.

4: Don’t schedule agents too frequently

> Run important checks hourly or a few times per day.
> Avoid running something every few minutes unless necessary.
> Use a cheap model for simple recurring jobs.
> Give each routine only the tools it needs.

Hermes cron jobs can even run a script first and skip calling the model completely when nothing has changed.

5: Give recurring work its own agent

> Keep your Chief of Staff for conversation and delegation.
> Create a separate agent for repetitive work.
> Give that the routine.
> Let its results appear in its own permanent chat.

This maps especially well to Hermes because routines belong to individual Bots and run in fresh sessions. 

6: Restrict what each agent is allowed to do

> Give each agent only the toolsets it needs.
> Allow reading by default.
> Restrict writing, deleting, buying or sending.
> Require approval for sensitive actions.
> Never give every Bot unrestricted computer access.

Hermes supports per-Bot toolsets/MCP servers, and Computer Use can run with a capability manifest that limits apps, websites and actions. 

7: Teach Hermes with examples of your work

> Give it examples of things you wrote yourself.
> Explain what you like about them.
> Put permanent style instructions in SOUL.md.
> Turn repeatable methods into Skills.
> Keep project-specific examples in the Project.

Hermes specifically separates identity/style in SOUL.md, user information in memory, project instructions in AGENTS.md, and reusable procedures in Skills.

8: Create a Chief of Agents

> Make one Bot called Chief of Staff or Chief of Agents.
> Give it your universal rules.
> Tell it which Bots handle which jobs.
> Tell it when it must ask you for approval.
> Use it to delegate work to your specialists.

Hermes Bots can directly @mention and hand work to other Bots, including Bots running on another machine.

9: Build routines like jobs for real employees

> Ask: “Could I give this task to a junior employee?” If yes, turn it into a routine.
> Define exactly what starts the job.
> Define what “finished” means.
> Run it only as often as the real-world task requires.

Good examples:

“Check my inbox every morning.”
“Find new leads twice per day.”
“Prepare my meeting brief at 7am.”
“Check competitors every afternoon.”

10: Name agents after exactly what they do

> Avoid names like “Bot 1”.
> Use names like Lead Finder.
> Inbox Cleaner.
> Research Analyst.
> Content Clipper.
> Chief of Staff.
> Then reinforce that job in the Bot description and SOUL.md.

And if you’re still scared to set up a Hermes agent then please read the thread below: 👇

here’s how you can run the full workflow by creating a buyer intent agent with hermes today: 👇 

1: Turn on the tools

> Run hermes tools.
> Enable X Search.
> Enable Web Search + Extract.

> Tell it its only job is finding people publicly showing buying intent.

> Your product.
> Your competitors.
> The problems you solve.
> Your ideal customer.
> Bad-fit customers to ignore.

Target founders and marketing leads at companies with 5–100 employees.”

> “alternative to [competitor]”
> “switching from [competitor]”
> “[competitor] is too expensive”
> “hate [competitor]”
> “[competitor] is frustrating”
> “what should I use instead of [competitor]”
> Direct complaints about the problem you solve.

Hermes has a dedicated x_search tool for public posts and threads. 

5: Mine the replies too

For every good post:

> Read the thread.
> Find replies agreeing with the complaint.
> Find people saying they have the same problem.
> Treat them as separate potential leads.

So one complaint might produce 5-10 prospects instead of one.

6: Remove rubbish

Tell Hermes:

> Ignore bots.
> Ignore obvious spam.
> Ignore competitor employees.
> Ignore joke posts.
> Ignore old complaints.
> Ignore people who clearly cannot buy the product.

7: Research each person

For every remaining lead:

> Search their name.
> Read their X bio.
> Find their role.
> Find their company.
> Find their company website.
> Never guess missing information.

8: Research their company

> What does the company do?
> Roughly how large is it?
> What industry is it in?
> Does it match our ICP?
> Could this person influence buying the product?

This can also replace what Amplemarket was doing but their job is to make it easier for you.

9: Score every lead

Give Hermes a simple score:

> Pain: /10
> Buying intent: /10
> ICP fit: /10
> Authority: /10
> Recency: /10

Then:

> Rank the strongest leads first.
> Drop weak leads.
> Only keep prospects above your chosen score.

10: Save everything

Simplest version:

> Create buyer-intent-leads.csv.
> Add each new lead as a row.
> Never add duplicates.

Columns:

> Name
> X account
> Company
> Role
> Original post
> Complaint
> Date
> Intent score
> ICP score
> Reason it matters
> Status

Hermes can read, search, create and edit local files itself. 

Move it to Google Sheets later.

11: Draft personalised outreach

For every strong lead:

> Read their exact complaint.
> Write a short public reply.
> Write a short DM.
> Reference what they actually said.
> Never use generic sales language.

For example:

“Saw your post about X being painful on Mac. We built Y specifically around that problem…”

12: Keep sending manual

Add this permanent rule:

“Never post, DM or email anyone without my approval.”

13: Test it

First say:

“Find me 20 buyer-intent leads from X from the last 7 days using this workflow.”

Then inspect the results. If they’re poor:

> Correct the scoring.
> Add exclusions.
> Improve search phrases.
> Tighten your ICP.

Do this until the leads are genuinely good.

Once it works:

> Ask Hermes to save the process as a Buyer Intent Skill.
> Include your searches, filters, scoring system and output format.

This means you don’t have to explain the whole workflow every time.

15: Make it automatic

Just ask it to schedule what you want!

$SNAP 𝗦𝗕𝗖: 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗘𝗟𝗘𝗣𝗛𝗔𝗡𝗧 𝗜𝗡 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗥𝗢𝗢𝗠

A lot of the criticism around $SNAP starts with stock-based compensation, and that criticism is fair. SBC is still high.

What I don’t agree with is the idea, repeated quite often on X, that Evan Spiegel has no incentive to see the stock go higher because he is simply using Snap as his personal piggy bank.

The facts point in the opposite direction.

SBC as a percentage of revenue has been steadily improving:

2023: ~29%
2024: ~19%
2025: ~17%
H1 2026: ~16%

More importantly, Spiegel himself has not been taking massive new stock grants. His billionaire status comes primarily from the Snap shares he already owns. Remove those shares and his net worth is likely measured in hundreds of millions, not billions.

Over the past three years, Evan Spiegel has received about $10.9 million in total reported compensation from Snap, virtually all of it security and travel-related benefits. He received $3 in total salary and $0 in new stock awards.

His economic incentive is therefore very simple: the higher $SNAP goes, the wealthier he becomes. If the stock continues falling, a large part of his wealth falls with it.

The problem has never really been Spiegel extracting billions from the company. The problem has been the company itself: too many employees, too much spending, excessive company-wide SBC and too much money directed toward projects that produced little shareholder value.

And that is exactly what makes Snap such an unusual investment situation.

Most companies in the stock market would probably envy this problem.

They need to invent new products, enter new markets, beat competitors or create new sources of revenue just to materially improve their economics.

Snap may not need to do much of that.

It mainly needs to stop doing what is unnecessary.

The process has already started. Snap recently cut roughly 16% of its workforce, around 1,000 employees, and eliminated more than 300 open positions. Management expects those actions to reduce its annualized cost base by more than $500 million by the second half of 2026.

AI provides another major tailwind. Smaller teams can increasingly do work that previously required much larger organizations. For a company where a large portion of SBC comes from R&D, that matters.

The investment case therefore doesn’t require heroic assumptions.

If revenue keeps growing while headcount, expenses and SBC continue falling as a percentage of revenue, operating leverage can improve very quickly.

That is Snap’s unusual position.

Most struggling companies need to figure out what they should start doing.

Snap may already have the product, the users and the revenue growth it needs.

It mostly needs to figure out what to stop doing.

And with an activist investor now in the room, there is finally another adult pushing management toward exactly that conclusion.

The biggest catalyst for $SNAP may not be what it creates next.

It may be what it finally stops wasting money on.

I keep getting asked: “How long are you planning to hold this stock?”

It’s a question I can’t really answer.

Imagine you just started dating someone and I ask, “How long are you going to stay with her?”

You’d probably say: I don’t know. Let’s see.

She looks good, acts well, talks well. That’s the initial thesis. But then you learn more. How does she behave with your parents? How does she treat people? How does she react when things don’t go her way?

Any one of those things can change the thesis.

Stocks are the same.

I could be out of $SNAP next quarter, even at $5, if I see that things are not developing the way I expected.

Or I could still be holding it at $20 if Evan Spiegel and management are actually making the changes I believe could unlock value.

Maybe you hold for a month. Maybe a year. Maybe ten years.

The holding period isn’t decided when I buy.

The thesis is.
And I hold for as long as the facts continue to support it.

𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗖𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗘𝗗 𝗣𝗢𝗥𝗧𝗙𝗢𝗟𝗜𝗢

Watch the Peter Lynch video below.

There have only been a handful of investors in history who consistently beat the market over very long periods.

Peter Lynch and Stanley Druckenmiller are probably somewhere in the top five, arguably top three.

And both have said versions of the same thing about concentration.

One of my biggest realizations over the last four years is that when I find an unusually obvious opportunity, I’m not afraid to concentrate.

I’m not saying you should wake up tomorrow and put 40% into a stock. Opportunities that justify that kind of concentration may come once a year, or once every two years.

But if you have done the work, understand the risks, and genuinely believe you have one of your best ideas in front of you, then owning 2% or 3% almost defeats the purpose.

If your best ideas are never at least 10% of your portfolio, you may be spending an enormous amount of time researching without allowing your best work to meaningfully affect your returns.

When I had around 40% in $ZIM, people called it reckless. But I was looking at a profitable company trading below the cash it held, with additional assets on top.

For me, taking money away from that opportunity simply to buy companies I understood much less, just for the sake of diversification, would have made even less sense.

People often point to hedge funds owning 40 or 50 stocks. But large funds have teams of analysts. Each analyst may really have only three or four highest-conviction ideas. Put 10 analysts together and suddenly the fund owns 40 stocks.

That is very different from one person pretending to deeply understand 40 companies.

Of course, this does not apply equally to every industry.

Biotech is a good example. Many biotech investments are closer to hero-or-zero outcomes, where one trial, one FDA decision or one safety issue can completely change the value of the company. In that kind of sector, diversification matters much more.

Concentration makes the most sense when you can actually understand and control the major variables of the thesis.

And when you really have an edge, your position has to be large enough for that edge to actually matter.

Of course, this does not apply equally to every industry.

Biotech is a good example. Many biotech investments are closer to hero-or-zero outcomes, where one trial, one FDA decision or one safety issue can completely change the value of the company. In that kind of sector, diversification matters much more.

Concentration makes the most sense when you can actually understand and control the major variables of the thesis.

And when you really have an edge, your position has to be large enough for that edge to actually matter.
